Variance-covariance matrix of a LaMaModel object

vcov.LaMaModel.Rd

Computes the approximate covariance matrix of the estimated parameters coef(object), either as the inverse Hessian of the negative log-likelihood at the estimate (type = "hessian"), or as a sandwich that remains valid if the model is misspecified: with the outer product of the scores (type = "sandwich"), heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (type = "HAC") or cluster-robust over tracks (type = "cluster").

Usage

# S3 method for class 'LaMaModel'
vcov(
  object,
  type = c("hessian", "sandwich", "HAC", "cluster"),
  kernel = c("QS", "Bartlett"),
  bw = NULL,
  cluster = NULL,
  cr = c("CR1", "CR0", "CR3", "CR3onestep"),
  ...
)

Arguments

object

model object of class "LaMaModel"

type

"hessian" (default) for the inverse Hessian, "sandwich" for the sandwich with the outer product of the scores, "HAC" for the HAC sandwich, or "cluster" for the cluster-robust sandwich

kernel

kernel of the HAC sandwich: "QS" (Quadratic Spectral, default) or "Bartlett" (Newey-West), see Details

bw

bandwidth of the HAC sandwich, a non-negative number. Defaults to the data-driven bandwidth of Andrews (1991) for the chosen kernel, see Details. For the Bartlett kernel, bw = L + 1 includes the lags up to \(L\), and bw at most 1 gives the same as type = "sandwich".

cluster

cluster identifier for type = "cluster", one value per observation (of any type, in the order of the observations in forward). Defaults to the tracks, i.e. the trackID reported by forward.

cr

small-sample adjustment for type = "cluster": "CR1" (default) multiplies the meat by \(G / (G - 1)\), "CR0" does not adjust, "CR3" is the jackknife, which refits the model without each cluster, and "CR3onestep" its approximation by one Newton step per cluster, see Details.

...

additional arguments (not used)

Value

covariance matrix with rows and columns named like coef(object)

Details

Hessian. The Hessian \(H\) is

  • the exact Hessian obj$he() for models without random effects,

  • for models with random effects, the Hessian of the Laplace-approximated marginal likelihood w.r.t. the fixed parameters, by finite differences of obj$gr() (as in sdreport),

  • for models from qreml, the Hessian of the penalised negative log-likelihood, including the penalised coefficients. The covariance is then conditional on the estimated smoothing parameters.

If the Hessian is not positive definite, which indicates that the model has not converged, a warning is issued.

Sandwich. With the per-observation score contributions \(u_t\) from scores, the covariance is \(H^{-1} M H^{-1}\) with the outer product of the scores as meat, \(M = \sum_t u_t u_t^\top\) (the outer product of gradients, OPG). It is robust to a misspecified predictive distribution as long as the \(u_t\) are serially uncorrelated, which they are under correct specification (martingale differences), but not to dependence the model misses. It equals the HAC sandwich with the Bartlett kernel and bw at most 1. Not to be confused with the inverse of the outer product alone, \(M^{-1}\) (the BHHH estimator), which, like \(H^{-1}\), is only valid under correct specification.

HAC sandwich. With the per-observation score contributions \(u_t\) from scores, the covariance is \(H^{-1} M H^{-1}\), with the kernel estimate of the variance of the score sum $$M = \Gamma_0 + \sum_{l \ge 1} k(l / b) (\Gamma_l + \Gamma_l^\top), \qquad \Gamma_l = \sum_t u_t u_{t-l}^\top,$$ where the sum in \(\Gamma_l\) only runs over pairs of observations from the same track (as reported by forward), as different tracks are independent. Missing observations contribute zero scores, so lags remain in units of time. The kernel \(k\) down-weights the autocovariances at longer lags, which are estimated with much noise, and the bandwidth \(b\) (bw) scales the lag axis. Two kernels are available:

  • kernel = "QS" (default), the Quadratic Spectral kernel $$k(x) = \frac{25}{12 \pi^2 x^2} \Bigl(\frac{\sin(6 \pi x / 5)}{6 \pi x / 5} - \cos(6 \pi x / 5)\Bigr).$$ Its weights are positive up to lag \(1.2 b\) and then oscillate with small amplitude, so all lags contribute. It is the most efficient kernel among those that guarantee a positive semi-definite \(M\) (Andrews, 1991): it keeps the short lags at nearly full weight, which reduces the bias.

  • kernel = "Bartlett", \(k(x) = \max(1 - |x|, 0)\), the Newey-West estimator: with \(b = L + 1\), lags up to \(L\) enter with weights \(1 - l / (L + 1)\).

The default bandwidth is the data-driven choice of Andrews (1991), which minimises the asymptotic mean squared error of \(M\) for an AR(1) approximation of the scores: with \(\rho_a\) and \(\sigma_a^2\) the coefficient and innovation variance of an AR(1) with intercept fitted to each score column \(a\) (by least squares on consecutive observations within tracks), $$b = 1.3221 \, (\alpha_2 \bar T)^{1/5} \; \text{(QS)}, \qquad b = 1.1447 \, (\alpha_1 \bar T)^{1/3} \; \text{(Bartlett)},$$ with \(\bar T\) the mean track length, \(\alpha_2 = \sum_a 4 \rho_a^2 \sigma_a^4 (1 - \rho_a)^{-8} / D\), \(\alpha_1 = \sum_a 4 \rho_a^2 \sigma_a^4 (1 - \rho_a)^{-6} (1 + \rho_a)^{-2} / D\) and \(D = \sum_a \sigma_a^4 (1 - \rho_a)^{-4}\). For a single track, this is sandwich::bwAndrews() without prewhitening and with equal weights. All score columns are weighted equally, so the bandwidth is driven by the most persistent and most variable ones. Stronger serial dependence of the scores gives a larger bandwidth.

All lags are computed exactly, with the fast Fourier transform within each track, which takes \(O(p T \log T + T p^2)\) operations for \(T\) observations and \(p\) parameters instead of \(O(T^2 p^2)\) for summing all lagged products directly.

If the model is correctly specified, the \(u_t\) are martingale differences, so \(\Gamma_l \approx 0\) for \(l \ge 1\) and \(M \approx H\): both types then agree approximately, and marked differences point to misspecification.

Cluster-robust sandwich. With the score sums \(s_k = \sum_{t \in k} u_t\) of the clusters \(k = 1, \dots, G\) (by default the tracks), the meat is $$M = c \sum_{k=1}^G s_k s_k^\top,$$ with \(c = 1\) (cr = "CR0") or \(c = G / (G - 1)\) (cr = "CR1", default). It makes no assumption about the dependence within clusters, so no bandwidth is needed, but requires independent clusters and is only reliable for many of them. As the \(s_k\) sum to the gradient, which is zero at the estimate, \(M\) has rank at most \(G - 1\), so the covariance is singular if \(G - 1\) is less than the number of parameters. For parameters informed by a single cluster only, such as track-specific initial distributions, it is not meaningful. Clusters may combine several tracks (e.g. several tracks of one individual), but a track must not be split between clusters.

cr = "CR3" gives the jackknife estimator (MacKinnon, Nielsen and Webb, 2023) $$V = \frac{G - 1}{G} \sum_{k=1}^G d_k d_k^\top, \qquad d_k = \hat\theta - \hat\theta^{(k)},$$ where \(\hat\theta^{(k)}\) is the estimate without cluster \(k\). It is found by minimising the weighted negative log-likelihood with weight zero on the observations of cluster \(k\), started at \(\hat\theta\), so the model is refitted once per cluster, and a message says so. Compared to CR1, it inflates the contributions of clusters with high leverage (e.g. long tracks), whose score sums are shrunk the most by fitting. Refits that do not converge give a warning. If the Hessian at the estimate of a refit is not positive definite, as for parameters not or only weakly identified without that cluster, an error is issued. That a refit has moved to another mode, for example with a different order of the states, is not checked; standard errors much larger than those of the one-step version can be a sign of this.

cr = "CR3onestep" approximates the change \(d_k\) by one Newton step from the estimate, $$d_k = (H - H_k)^{-1} s_k,$$ where \(H - H_k\) is the Hessian without cluster \(k\), from the weighted likelihood with weight zero on its observations. It costs one Hessian per cluster and no refits. For linear least squares, the step is exact; otherwise, the approximation is poorest if there are few clusters or if one of them carries much of the information. With equal leverage \(H_k = H / G\), it coincides with CR1. The one-step deletion is a pure Newton step, so it requires \(H - H_k\) to be positive definite: if leaving out a cluster makes it singular or indefinite, an error is issued.

All sandwiches require the likelihood function to call forward once (with trackID for several tracks) and are not available for models with random effects or from qreml.

References

Andrews, D. W. K. (1991). Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix estimation. Econometrica, 59(3), 817–858.

Newey, W. K. and West, K. D. (1987). A simple, positive semi-definite, heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix. Econometrica, 55(3), 703–708.

MacKinnon, J. G., Nielsen, M. O. and Webb, M. D. (2023). Cluster-robust inference: A guide to empirical practice. Journal of Econometrics, 232(2), 272–299.

Cameron, A. C. and Miller, D. L. (2015). A practitioner's guide to cluster-robust inference. Journal of Human Resources, 50(2), 317–372.
